title: Cicero duty override binds a promise to recipient and common-good harm
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED, NOT SELECTED. Cicero De officiis III.95 gives a compact nested condition: a promise or entrusted object is normally returned, but the obligation is suspended when the recipient is insane or the entrusted money would support war against the common country; coercion and deceit also void the promise. A finite evaluator binds promise, recipient, public-good status, and coercion/deceit flags, producing WITHHOLD or PERFORM. An unconditional-promise rival yields the opposite outcome on the source examples.

source.source_span: Complete bounded argument: promises/trusts can cease to bind when circumstances change; a sword left by a sane person is not returned when he is insane, and entrusted money is not returned when the recipient would wage war against the common country.
source.provenance: Perseus provides the Latin/English De officiis III.95 passage and identifies the 1913 Miller edition. The examples are source claims, not a general modern ethics rule or target Vorlage.

duplicate_screen.checked: IDEA000028 generic modal obligation; IDEA000335 Benedict fault/re-entry; IDEA000446 Pliny rescript policy cursor; route-check obligation/condition.
duplicate_screen.difference: This is a parameterized exception to an existing promise, with two independently bound harm dimensions and an explicit priority rule. It does not model monastic status, administrative reply, or a record lifecycle.

operators: OVERRIDE(promise, harm_recipient, harm_common, coercion, deceit) -> DUTY_RESULT
rules: First reject coercion or deceit: the promise is VOID.
Otherwise, if returning the object harms its recipient OR the common good, return WITHHOLD.
Only when both harm flags are false does the normal promise result become PERFORM.
constructor.rival: ALWAYS_PERFORM returns PERFORM for all three cases; it cannot represent Cicero's changed duty when the bound recipient/common-good parameter changes.
constructor.observable_consequence: Changing only the bound harm parameter flips the result from PERFORM to WITHHOLD while preserving the same promise/object frame. The two source examples therefore share one obligation rule but differ in which parameter triggers the override.
constructor.falsifier: Reject if the same harm parameter must both preserve and suspend a promise under one declared context, or if the evaluator needs an unlisted recipient/object to decide. The source does not quantify harm or identify any target form.
constructor.target_binding_limit: No target gloss or source-to-target promise mapping is claimed.
